title: Best Glycolic Acid Serums for Dark Spots and Hyperpigmentation (2026)
summary: The best glycolic acid serum for dark spots pairs glycolic with pigment-fighting actives like tranexamic and azelaic acid, used nightly with daily SPF.
body_markdown:
Glycolic acid is one of the most reliable over-the-counter ingredients for fading dark spots, and a good serum makes it easy to use at home. Here's what actually works, and how to choose.


## Quick Answer


The best glycolic acid serum for dark spots is one that pairs glycolic acid's surface exfoliation with actives that target pigment directly, such as tranexamic and azelaic acid. Glycolic acid speeds the shedding of pigment-laden surface cells, so spots fade faster, but on its own it works mainly on the top layer. Our top pick is **Lion Pose UNSPOTTED 4X Acid Jelly Night Serum** (~$79), a multi-acid night serum that combines glycolic and lactic acids with tranexamic acid, azelaic acid, niacinamide, and glutathione. Whatever you choose, use it at night and wear a broad-spectrum SPF 30+ every morning, or new spots will keep forming.


## Does glycolic acid fade dark spots?


Yes, glycolic acid fades dark spots by exfoliating the pigmented surface layer of skin faster than it would shed on its own. The[American Academy of Dermatology](https://www.aad.org/public/everyday-care/skin-care-secrets/routine/fade-dark-spots) lists glycolic acid among the ingredients that "can fade existing dark spots," alongside azelaic acid, kojic acid, retinoids, and vitamin C. Because dark spots are clusters of excess melanin sitting in the upper skin, speeding cell turnover helps carry that pigment to the surface and away.


The catch is depth. Glycolic acid works best on pigment held in the epidermis (the outer layer). Deeper, dermal pigment — common in stubborn melasma — responds more slowly and usually needs pigment-specific actives layered in, which is why single-ingredient glycolic products fade surface spots but stall on the deep ones.


## How does glycolic acid work on hyperpigmentation?


Glycolic acid works on hyperpigmentation by loosening the "glue" between dead surface skin cells, which accelerates exfoliation and turnover. It is the smallest alpha hydroxy acid (AHA), derived from sugar cane, and its low molecular weight lets it penetrate the outer skin efficiently and act as a chemical exfoliant. As pigmented corneocytes shed and turnover speeds up, discoloration lifts and skin tone looks more even.


Glycolic acid also improves how well other brightening ingredients absorb, so it earns its place in a routine as much for what it enables as for what it does alone. In dermatology offices, higher-strength glycolic acid peels have long been used as an adjunct treatment for melasma and general hyperpigmentation. At-home serum concentrations are gentler and slower, which is exactly what you want for daily use.


## What strength of glycolic acid do you need for dark spots?


For at-home dark-spot care, glycolic acid serums in roughly the 5–10% range are effective and tolerable for most people. Lower strengths (around 5–7%) suit sensitive or reactive skin and daily use, while 8–10% formulas resurface more aggressively and are typically used a few nights a week. Higher in-office peels (30–70%) exist but are performed by professionals, not applied at home.


Concentration is only part of the story: pH and formulation matter just as much. A well-buffered 10% serum can be gentler than a poorly formulated 8% one. The key difference for dark spots specifically is whether the product also includes pigment-targeting actives — a serum that combines glycolic with tranexamic or azelaic acid does more for discoloration than glycolic alone.

## How do you use a glycolic acid serum safely?


Use a glycolic acid serum at night, starting two to three times a week and building up as your skin tolerates it. Apply to clean, dry skin before moisturizer, and avoid layering it with other strong exfoliants or retinoids on the same night when you're starting out, which can trigger irritation. If you feel stinging beyond a brief tingle, cut back the frequency.


The single most important step is daily sunscreen. The American Academy of Dermatology stresses that treating dark spots "begins with sunscreen," recommending a broad-spectrum SPF 30 or higher — ideally a tinted formula with iron oxide for extra protection against the visible light that worsens melasma. Without it, glycolic acid can leave freshly resurfaced skin more vulnerable to new pigment, undoing your progress.


## Frequently Asked Questions


### How long does glycolic acid take to fade dark spots?


Most surface dark spots take a few weeks to a few months to visibly lighten with consistent nightly use. The American Academy of Dermatology notes that a spot a few shades darker than your skin usually fades within 6 to 12 months, while deeper discoloration can take longer. Daily sunscreen is essential, or new spots offset your progress.


### Can you use a glycolic acid serum every night?


Some people tolerate glycolic acid nightly, but most should start two to three nights a week and increase gradually. Building up slowly lets your skin barrier adjust and reduces the risk of redness, stinging, or peeling. If you notice irritation, scale back frequency rather than pushing through, and always follow with morning SPF.


### Is glycolic acid safe for darker skin tones?


Glycolic acid can be used on darker skin tones, but with extra care, because Fitzpatrick IV–VI skin is more prone to post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation. Start at a low strength, go slow, and avoid over-exfoliating, since irritation itself can trigger new dark marks. A gentler multi-acid serum with soothing niacinamide is often a safer bet than a high-percentage single acid.


### Glycolic acid vs. vitamin C for dark spots — which works better?


Glycolic acid and vitamin C fade dark spots differently and work well together, not against each other. Glycolic exfoliates pigmented surface cells, while vitamin C is an antioxidant that helps brighten and interrupt melanin production. For faster results, many people use a vitamin C serum in the morning and a glycolic-based serum at night.


### Can you use glycolic acid with retinol or niacinamide?


Niacinamide pairs well with glycolic acid and can make routines gentler, so combining them is fine for most people. Retinol plus glycolic acid on the same night can be too much for sensitive skin and may cause irritation, so many dermatologists suggest alternating nights. Introduce one active at a time to see how your skin responds.


## The Bottom Line


Glycolic acid is a proven, accessible way to fade dark spots, working by speeding up how quickly your skin sheds pigmented surface cells. The best serums go a step further and pair it with actives that target pigment at the source, which is why a multi-acid formula tends to outperform glycolic on its own for discoloration.


If you want one product that covers surface and deeper spots, start with a multi-acid night serum like UNSPOTTED, use it consistently, and protect your progress with daily broad-spectrum sunscreen. Fading pigment is a marathon, not a sprint — give any routine at least eight to twelve weeks before judging results.


*This article is for educational purposes only and is not a substitute for professional medical advice. If you have persistent hyperpigmentation, melasma, or sensitive skin, consult a board-certified dermatologist before starting a new treatment.*
